Admission Diagnosis: Palpitation

Discharge Diagnosis: Interatrial Septal Mass Wrapped in Interatrial Septum, Secundum Atrial Septal Defect, Heterogeneous Echogenicity and Incomplete Right Bundle Branch Block.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a complaint of palpitation for 30 days. The physical examination did not reveal any abnormalities. A routine 12-lead ECG showed atrial premature beats and sinus rhythm. A further 24-hours holter detected sinus arrhythmia, incomplete right bundle branch block, atrial premature beats, and paroxysmal atrial tachycardia. Following the recommendation of TTE, a circular mass measuring 3.4 × 3.4 cm was detected that was attached to the interatrial septum protruding to the right atrium. TEE confirms the mass location close to the superior vena cava with no obstructing venous drainage. It was observed that the mass did not show good mobility on TEE. A 6 mm secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right shunting was also detected below the mass. The atria and ventricle size appeared to be normal, and there was no observed valvular dysfunction or thrombus. Computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a high-intensity nodular and annular shadow around the inner wall with heterogeneous density inside. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was unable to provide a clear view of the interatrial septum. A cardiopulmonary bypass cardiac surgery was performed to remove the interatrial septal mass. Intraoperation, the mass was found to have a smooth and rough surface on the left and right atrial sides, respectively, and was entirely removed intact. An artificial patch was used to suture and close the defect and ASD. The pathology of the mass proved to be organized thrombus with calcium deposition and fibrinoid necrosis. The ECG after surgery showed sinus rhythm and IBBB without atrioventricular block. The patient was discharged with oral aspirin for 3 months, and follow-up was planned as an outpatient.

Discharge Medications:

Oral Aspirin.

Follow-up:

Follow-up was planned as an outpatient.

Discharge Condition:

Stable.

The patient, a 17-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital with a history of nodular sclerosis-type Hodgkin lymphoma. After infusion, the patient's condition was complicated by the rapid accumulation of pericardial and pleural effusions. She was found to have cytomegalovirus reactivation, and polyomavirus BK viruria caused grade III hemorrhagic cystitis. The patient required a tracheostomy and suffered from episodes of complex partial seizures. Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple infarct-like lesions. The patient was later diagnosed with rapidly progressive hypercalcemia and hospice care was required. The patient passed away on day +94.

Throughout the patient's hospital course, there was no evidence of acute GVHD, and complete donor chimerism was documented until day +89. The patient was given ganciclovir, a total of 7 doses of intravenous immunoglobulins from day +37 to day +69, and cyclosporine and mycophenolate mofetil were given from day +5 for GVHD prophylaxis. Hemodialysis was discontinued after day +76, and no attacks of seizure/severe hypertension occurred after day +80.

Outcome:

The patient's condition was complicated by multiple complications, leading to a poor prognosis. Hospice care was required, and the patient passed away on day +94.

The patient, a 28-year-old female, was admitted because of brown pigmentation and sclerosis of the right lower limb. She had a past medical history of Caesarean sections, without particular familial medical history. Upon first examination, brown pigmentation with a slightly clear boundary was present on the right thigh and crus. No general symptoms, such as Raynaud's phenomenon, were noted. 

Histopathological examination revealed flattened epidermis in the sclerotic region and increased collagen fibers directly below the epidermis over the deep dermis. Appendages, such as sweat glands, had been lost in this region. In the pigmented region, many infiltrating inflammatory cells were noted around sweat glands, vessels, and adipose tissue in the deep dermis. Melanin deposits were noted throughout the epidermal layer in the pigmented area. 

The patient was diagnosed with localized scleroderma and oral treatment with etretinate 20 mg/day was initiated. The skin sclerosis started to improve 28 days after treatment initiation. Topical corticosteroids were not administered during this period, and no adverse events developed. 

15 months after the discontinuation of etretinate treatment, although brown pigmentation remained, improvements in skin eruption were maintained compared to those upon first examination. Biopsy results showed epidermal thickening, presence of sweat glands in the dermis, and bulky and dense collagen fibers in the dermis. Under high magnification, infiltrating inflammatory cells around vessels and in lobular fat in the deep dermis had decreased and atrophied appendages had recovered. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Localized Scleroderma

Discharge Medications: None

Follow-up: The patient will follow up with the dermatologist for continued monitoring of the brown pigmentation and sclerosis on the right lower limb. She will be instructed on proper skincare and sun protection measures.

The patient presented with painful perineal ulcers and a history of Crohn's disease (CD) diagnosed overseas. He was non-compliant with therapy and developed recurrent perianal abscesses and fistulas requiring drainage and seton placement. The initial biopsy showed inflammatory infiltrate but no cell atypia, and tissue cultures for bacteria, acid fast bacilli, and fungi were negative. The working diagnosis at the time was pyoderma gangrenosum, but the patient noticed some improvement in his perineal pain without intervention and elected to continue with expectant management.

MRI of the pelvis was organized, which showed evidence of a tract adjoining the left groin to the perineum, along with a medial branch extending towards the rectum. The tract was drained via the perineal opening, and a seton was inserted to allow drainage and healing of the complex fistula.

In the coming months, the patient experienced intermittent PR bleeding and lower abdominal pain despite compliance with mesalazine. Infliximab was started for the presumed flare of CD. However, before his second dose of infliximab, ulcerations in the perineal region recurred. At this time, he also developed papulopustular lesions over his arms and inner thighs alongside oral ulcerations. He was referred to a rheumatologist with investigations revealing HLA B51 and HLA B27 positivity. The diagnostic criteria for BS was subsequently met, and a plan for tailored therapy was initiated.

- Patient presented with worsening painful perineal ulcers on a background of Crohn's disease.
- Biopsy showed inflammatory infiltrate but no cell atypia, and tissue cultures were negative.

Patient Name: [redacted]
Age: 83
Sex: Female
Admission Date: April 2016
Discharge Date: N/A

Hospital Course Summary:

An 83-year-old female patient was admitted due to heart failure caused by severe aortic stenosis (AS) and repetitive bleeding episodes, necessitating blood transfusions. The patient had been diagnosed with AS in 2014 and had progressively worsening AS with a mean aortic valve pressure gradient of 81 mmHg, peak aortic flow of 5.61 m/s, and aortic valve area of 0.5 cm2. The patient experienced bleeding from angiodysplasia in the stomach, which required endoscopic argon plasma coagulation (APC) for hemostasis, but she continued to have repetitive bleeding episodes even after treatment. The plasma analysis revealed the deficiency of high molecular weight (HMW) multimers of VWF, which was defined as the 11th and the upper bands in the VWF multimer analysis. Thus, the patient was diagnosed with Heyde's syndrome.

Due to the patient's frailty with primary biliary cirrhosis-associated liver dysfunction, a transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was performed with a 23-mm Edwards Sapien 3 valve (Edwards Lifesciences, Irvine, California). The patient's aortic valve area and mean aortic valve pressure gradient showed immediate improvements from 0.5 cm2 to 1.5 cm2 and from 81 mmHg to 10 mmHg, respectively. Following the TAVI procedure, the patient received heparin only during the perioperative period and was treated with clopidogrel at 75 mg/day, starting one week after TAVI. An endoscopy at 10 days after TAVI showed remaining angiodysplasia but no further bleeding in the stomach. Since the TAVI procedure, the patient has had no more episodes of anemia originating from angiodysplasia in the stomach. Notably, there was a clear disappearance of angiodysplasia at 4 months after TAVI. Moreover, HMW multimers of VWF showed immediate and persistent recovery after TAVI. The patient was maintained on clopidogrel therapy and, up to 2 years after TAVI, there were no reported episodes of bleeding or thromboembolic events. A follow-up endoscopy showed that the patient remained free of angiodysplasia in the stomach.

In summary, the patient was admitted to the hospital due to heart failure with repetitive bleeding episodes and was diagnosed with Heyde's syndrome. The patient had a successful TAVI with an Edwards Sapien 3 valve and showed rapid and persistent improvements in both the aortic valve area and the mean aortic valve pressure gradient. Following the procedure and a few weeks of clopidogrel therapy, there were no further episodes of anemia due to angiodysplasia in the stomach, and the patient had no reports of bleeding or thromboembolic events up to 2 years after TAVI.

Pulsatile headache accompanied by nausea and occasional vomiting with fever.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 42-year-old woman, was admitted due to a persistent pulsatile headache accompanied by nausea and occasional vomiting with fever. She had a known history of migraine and tension-type headaches. An evaluation was carried out to identify the underlying cause of the headache, which included neurological examination, laboratory data from blood and spinal fluid, and several imaging tests such as a contrast-enhanced head magnetic resonance imaging and computed tomography angiography. After evaluation, diagnosis of meningitis was suspected and ruled out after confirming that none of the data indicated an abnormality that could explain the headache.
During the hospitalization, change in the nature of the headache occurred. It tightened around the entire head and nausea appeared in addition to headache while mild occipital pain remained. Possibility of occipital neuralgia was considered and treatment with 400 mg of oral carbamazepine was commenced, which resulted in symptom relief. Later, the patient developed symptoms of trismus, facial nerve paralysis, stiffness of the tongue base, photophobia, and cardiac autonomic nervous disorder. Based on the characteristic symptoms, the patient was diagnosed with tetanus and treated accordingly with tetanus toxoid vaccine, human tetanus immunoglobulin, and penicillin G.
After the treatment, the remaining headache that encircled the whole head improved and an occipital headache remained. During the subsequent course of the disease, the patient developed various symptoms which gradually improved. She started to report palpitations under mild exertion, which improved after an autonomic dysfunction was confirmed by the electrocardiogram test.

Summary:
The patient, a 42-year-old woman, was admitted for a persistent pulsatile headache with nausea and occasional vomiting accompanied by fever. After extensive evaluation, a diagnosis of tetanus was confirmed, and treatment resulted in symptom relief. The patient developed trismus, facial nerve paralysis, stiffness of the tongue base, photophobia, and cardiac autonomic nervous disorder during the course of the disease, which gradually improved. She reported palpitations under mild exertion, which was confirmed by an electrocardiogram test. The patient was discharged in an improved condition and advised to follow-up as an outpatient.

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted due to severe abdominal pain along with high-grade fever and turbid effluent.

Hospital Course:
The patient had end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy and had been on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) using the Twin Bag system (Baxter HealthCare, McGaw Park, Illinois, USA) for 6 years. He had a history of bacterial peritonitis 3 years after starting on CAPD which was managed successfully with antibiotics. At presentation, the patient was febrile with a diffusely tender abdomen. His CAPD fluid analysis showed 1050 cells with 75% polymorphs while the fluid culture was sterile. The i.v. meropenem and vancomycin antibiotics he had received for 48 hours prior to presenting to the hospital were continued. Repeat CAPD effluent bacterial and fungal cultures, acid-fast staining, and mycobacterial culture (collected later) were sterile. However, in the absence of response, the patient's CAPD catheter was removed 72 hours after initial treatment. The patient continued on i.v. antibiotics with no improvement. One week post-admission, an ultrasound (USG) of the abdomen revealed loculated ascites, which was drained via USG-guided ascitic tap. Due to the persistence of fever and loculated pus collections, the patient underwent open laparotomy revealing multiple loculated fluid collections with dense adhesions between bowel loops and peritoneum. The loculi were broken, and about 500 ml of pus was drained. During the laparotomy, the peritoneal and omental biopsy revealed large areas of necrosis along with broad aseptate fungal hyphae consistent with zygomycosis. The patient was started on i.v. conventional amphotericin B and showed improvement 48 hours later and was afebrile. He received a total of 3 g amphotericin B and was discharged after 6 months of follow-up.

Diagnosis:
End-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy, bacterial peritonitis, loculated ascites, zygomycosis.

Treatment:
Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD), i.v. meropenem, i.v. vancomycin, open laparotomy, i.v. conventional amphotericin B.

The patient was doing fine at 6 months follow-up.

The patient history was consistent with well-differentiated appendiceal mucinous cystadenocarcinoma.

The patient, a 33-year-old Caucasian female, was admitted to the orthopedic outpatient clinic in October 2001, with complaints of chronic pain in the left hip since 1997. Her medical history showed two episodes of pleuritis and infertility problems. The patient lived a healthy life, was a non-smoker and drank 2 units of alcohol per week.

Upon initial physical examination, all hip joint movements were limited and painful. Hematological blood testing revealed a total white blood count of 9.4/cu mm and ESR of 30 mm in the first hour. Conventional hip radiography showed some osseous destruction of the joint with narrowing of the joint space, suggesting loss of articular cartilage. Additional imaging showed osteonecrosis, destruction of the hip joint, periarticular oedema, and multiple fluid collections.

The patient underwent an open biopsy, which revealed granulation tissue and destruction of the cartilage of the femoral head, suggesting articular tuberculosis. Ziehl-Nielsen staining of the debris was positive for acid-fast bacilli. A Mantoux-test was performed, which was strongly positive. The patient was treated with tuberculostatics for 12 months.

Filling of the acetabular defect resulting from ankylosis with the femoral head occurred approximately 4 months after initiation of chemotherapy and immobilization. In November 2003, a primary one-stage cementless total hip arthroplasty was performed. Histopathological examination of the retrieved bone and joint capsule showed no signs of tuberculosis. Therefore, postoperatively she did not receive any tuberculostatics. No peri or postoperative complications occurred.

At the latest follow up in March 2008, 52 months after total hip replacement, no signs of reactivation of the tuberculosis were present. The patient experienced no pain and had a normal range of motion. She did not suffer from any significant limitations in her daily activities, including sports and labour. The bone that formerly belonged to the femoral head had fully integrated with the acetabulum. Radiological assessment of the left hip showed no signs of loosening. The patient was discharged from the hospital in November 2003.

The patient, a 33-year-old Caucasian female, was admitted to the orthopedic outpatient clinic with chronic pain in the left hip since 1997. She was diagnosed with articular tuberculosis and was treated with tuberculostatics for 12 months. A primary one-stage cementless total hip arthroplasty was performed and the patient was discharged in November 2003. At the latest follow up, no signs of reactivation of the tuberculosis were present and radiological assessment of the left hip showed no signs of loosening.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Sex: Female
Age: 3 years

Diagnosis:
- Arnold-Chiari type 2 malformation
- Recurrent urinary tract infections and voiding dysfunction
- Right renal staghorn calculus

Hospital Course:

The 3-year-old female child was admitted to our clinic with a diagnosis of Arnold-Chiari type 2 malformation and recurrent urinary tract infections with voiding dysfunction. The patient had a past surgical history of meningomyelocele and anal atresia and had undergone cystolithotripsy procedure due to two bladder stones six months ago. The ultrasound examination showed multiple stones in the right kidney with the largest one measuring 24mm in diameter and left-sided renal atrophy. Percutaneous nephrostomy catheter was placed into the collecting system of the right kidney, and mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy was planned for the right kidney stones after a sterile urine culture. Urogenital septum dividing the bladder and vagina was detected during cystoscopy. A ureteroscopy was performed before starting percutaneous nephrolithotomy, and the stones were fragmented with laser and pneumatic lithotripter. A residual stone of 5mm in size was seen and a 3cm 8F Malecot nephrostomy tube was introduced to the right kidney. The procedure was terminated after Foley urethral catheter was inserted. The total surgical time was 105 minutes.

The patient was discharged from the hospital after one week. Within six months, there were no residual or recurrent renal stones. Informed written consent was obtained from the patient's family regarding the publication of the case study.

Impression and Plan:

The 3-year-old female child with Arnold-Chiari type 2 malformation and recurrent urinary tract infections with voiding dysfunction was treated successfully with mini-percutaneous nephrolithotomy and discharged from the hospital after one week. The patient was advised to follow-up with the physician regularly and comply with the advised preventive measures and medications to prevent recurrence of the renal stones.

65-year-old male was brought to the emergency department after a motorbike accident. Vital signs were stable, and the patient was alert and cooperative. Physical examination revealed decreased respiratory murmurs bilaterally and abdominal tenderness with a loss-of-substance lesion detected on inspection. Blood-gas analysis showed mild acidosis and elevated lactate. Total body CT scan showed decomposed fractures of multiple ribs, a complete herniation of the stomach into the left thorax, a left parietal face laceration, and mild subarachnoid hemorrhage. The patient underwent a median laparotomy which revealed a laceration of the left diaphragm and a penetrating abdominal trauma. Both the diaphragmatic and abdominal lesions were repaired with suture using non-absorbable monofilament polypropylene. Subsequently, the patient developed hyperpyrexia, ongoing left pleural effusion and underwent a temporary tracheostomy. On the tenth post-operative day, a negative pressure wound therapy device was applied to treat the wound in the upper left region. Post-operative day twenty revealed an enteric liquid that was later found to be a direct communication in an entero-cutaneous fistula. In view of the impossibility to restore normal bowel function and obtain healing of the abdominal wound, a segmentary colonic and cutaneous en-bloc resection was performed, followed by a side-to-side colo-colic anastomosis, and reconstruction of the anterior abdominal wall with a biological mesh. The patient was discharged after 63 days with completely restored bowel function. An abdominal CT scan obtained ten months later revealed an uncomplicated incisional hernia in the site of the previous trauma.

The patient presented with amenorrhea and bleeding per vaginum after attempting first-trimester abortion using over-the-counter drugs. She experienced blurring of vision, mild occipital headache, and vomiting, which progressively worsened. The patient was admitted to the ophthalmology department with a diagnosis of Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy. Raised intracranial pressure was suspected as the cause of papilledema and vision loss. 

The patient was evaluated and treated for severe anemia, and received four red blood cell transfusions. Lumbar puncture was performed, and the cerebrospinal fluid analysis for infective and malignant causes was negative. Non-contrast CT and MRI were unremarkable, which confirmed the absence of neurological pathology. 

Methylprednisolone was administered to improve vision due to intracranial hypotension. The patient's vision improved with repeated lumbar puncture but only hand movements were detected in her left eye. Repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture and optic nerve sheath fenestration were performed on day 16. Papilledema and visual acuity improved significantly after the procedure. 

The patient's BMI increased during the hospital course. She was discharged on oral hematinics and acetazolamide with continued monitoring for anemia and vision checks.

• Admitted with Amenorrhea and bleeding per vaginum after attempting first-trimester abortion.
• Developed Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy with bilateral visual loss.
• Elevated intracranial pressure suspected as cause of papilledema and vision loss.
• Investigated and treated for severe anemia with a total of four red blood cell transfusions.
• Methylprednisolone administration for intracranial hypotension to improve vision.
• Repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture and optic nerve sheath fenestration performed to improve visual acuity.

The patient's diet was gradually increased from liquid to normal starting from the fifth postoperative day. The patient's occlusion was stabilized after completion of the postsurgical orthodontic and bilateral molar occlusal reconstruction. The results of cephalometric analysis at 1 month after the operation showed an overbite of 2 mm and an overjet of 2.5 mm.

The patient reported satisfaction at being able to use his front teeth when eating and that others had observed that he was laughing more frequently. The occlusion is currently stable and the patient reports that it is no longer hindering his daily life. The patient's follow-up was continued on an outpatient basis to 5 years after surgery.

Discharge Plan:

The patient was successfully discharged from our hospital 3 days after surgery. Piperacillin sodium was administered by intravenous infusion at 1 g x 2/day for 3 days. The patient was advised to maintain a normal diet and to continue using orthodontic elastics as directed. The patient was also advised to continue his follow-up on an outpatient basis every few weeks for the next 3 months.

The patient had a peripherally inserted central venous catheter inserted for total parenteral nutrition 11 days before the onset of symptoms. The patient was given azithromycin but continued to have persistent symptoms, which led to hospitalization. The initial chest x-ray demonstrated diffuse, peripherally located reticulonodular infiltrates in both lung fields, and laboratory testing showed an elevated white blood cell count. The patient was admitted to the hospital, and two sets of blood cultures showed bacterial growth with gram-positive cocci in clusters reported on gram stain.

The patient was started on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for community-acquired pneumonia, and vancomycin and oseltamivir were added due to concern for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia and a preceding influenza-like illness. The patient continued to have persistent symptoms and developed thrombosis in the right brachial vein, which led to the administration of heparin for anticoagulation and the addition of clindamycin to the antibiotic regimen. The patient was transferred to the University of Chicago Medical Center for further care, where her microbiology cultures showed Kocuria kristinae. Antimicrobial susceptibilities were performed on the isolates and found to be positive. Septic emboli seen on CT were felt to be secondary to septic thrombosis complicating a catheter-related bloodstream infection. Oxacillin was started, and vancomycin and clindamycin were discontinued. The patient continued to improve, and she was discharged home on hospital day 16 to complete a 4-week course of intravenous oxacillin for complicated bacteremia with enoxaparin for anticoagulation for a duration of 6 months.

Patient V-4, a 5-year-old Moroccan boy, was admitted to the hospital for the evaluation and treatment of familial epilepsy. The patient had a history of neonatal hypotonia, psychomotor delay, and daily-generalized seizures that began at 8 months old and had not responded to treatment with valproate of sodium. At the time of admission, the patient had a delay in stature and weight, microcephaly, and severe hypotonia, without any facial dysmorphia or nystagmus. A CT scan showed no abnormalities, but an EEG showed abnormal waves in the right fronto-temporal region.

Family history revealed that five cousins and two maternal uncles had also been diagnosed with epilepsy, and some had experienced neonatal hypotonia and psychomotor delay. Four family members had died at a young age from their epilepsy. In an effort to identify a causal mutation, whole-exome sequencing was performed for the patient and his cousin, and a hemizygous base substitution was identified in the PLP1 gene, c.251C > A (p.Ala84Asp). This mutation was found to co-segregate with the disease phenotype in the affected subjects and the carriers in the family.

The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of familial epilepsy associated with a mutation in the PLP1 gene, and the family was advised to undergo genetic counseling. Further testing for the mutation was also recommended for family members who had not yet been tested. The patient's parents were counseled on continued management of the patient's epilepsy and referred to a neurologist for ongoing care. The patient was also scheduled for regular follow-up with the neurologist to monitor his condition and adjust his treatment as needed.
